 When police officers found two dead bodies beside dog kennels at a Colleton County farm on the night of June 7, 2021, they initially suspected the victims were 22-year-old Paul Murdaugh and his girlfriend.
 Soon enough, however, it became clear that Paul, the scion of an influential Lowcountry family, had been shot to death with his mother, Maggie Murdaugh.
 The next day, police and a local prosecutor walked the crime scene and were puzzled as to how a pair of spent shotgun shells were found sitting inside a feed room beside the dog kennels, as all other evidence indicated Paul Murdaugh was shot from outside the feed room as he stood in the doorway.
 Investigators later realized a gap existed between the bottom of the door and the floor of the feed room that was tall enough for a shotgun shell to roll under, according to recently released records from the State Law Enforcement Division.
 The infamous, long-running Murdaugh murder saga has generated much mystery, only a portion of which has been resolved.
 In April, confessed swindler and disbarred lawyer Alex Murdaugh is scheduled to be tried a second time for the murders of his wife and younger son. The retrial was ordered by the S.C. Supreme Court because of prejudicial comments made to jurors by a Colleton County court official during Murdaugh’s original double-murder trial in 2023, in which he was convicted of the killings.
 As the retrial approaches, law enforcement’s previous and lingering confusion over the crime is taking center stage.
 Murdaugh’s lawyers have filed a motion asking Judge Debra McCaslin to dismiss the double-murder indictment because of incorrect information told to grand jurors by the lead investigator on the case.
 Before Murdaugh was accused of slaughtering his family, lead SLED agent David Owen testified to grand jurors that blood spatter was found on the T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the murder. In fact, no blood spatter was detected.
 Owen also testified that Murdaugh family shotguns were all found preloaded with two shells — one buckshot and one birdshot — just like the suspected murder weapon. This, too, was untrue.
 In anticipation of this issue being argued at a Nov. 13 pre-trial hearing in Lexington, state prosecutors have denied any fabrication or falsification of evidence. Moreover, they say, grand jurors rightfully indicted Murdaugh because there was “more than ample probable cause regardless of whether that (incorrect) evidence is considered or not.”
 The judge must decide: Are these alleged errors so prejudicial that the entire foundation of the state’s case against Murdaugh is unsound and unfair?
 Tips galore
 In Murdaughland, almost nothing is straightforward .
 For more than a decade, Murdaugh deceived legal clients and loved ones and stole millions from them.
 As his deceptions came to light, he allegedly staged a roadside shooting with a friend in which Murdaugh claimed to be a victim of an unknown attacker who shot him in the head.
 Murdaugh also told investigators that he never went to the dog kennels on his farm the night of the murders, though a video found on his son’s cellphone revealed this to be untrue.
 All these lies clouded the reality of a weird, multifaceted, Southern Gothic crime spree associated with Murdaugh and his family that includes elements of massive fraud, illegal drugs, suspicious deaths, murder, witness manipulation, fabricated allegations and a deadly, drunken boat crash.
 Bullet holes are seen in the glass of the feed room at the Murdaugh family’s Moselle property on Wednesday, March 1, 2023, in Islandton.
 File/Staff 
 As police sought to distinguish fact from fiction, they not only had to investigate Murdaugh’s many false claims but also plenty of tips from other people, according to SLED’s case history, which contains a log of the tips.
 SLED received word from neighbors of a Murdaugh family property that they obtained photos of supposedly suspicious vehicles parked nearby, according to a SLED case history authored by Owen.
 Police investigated a tip that a farm caretaker was somehow involved in the murders, as well as a claim that a man had befriended Maggie Murdaugh through the virtual reality game Second Life.
 There was a tip from a South Carolina prison inmate about a pair of alleged methamphetamine users shopping for illegal drugs while possessing a notepad on which the murder victims’ names — “Maggie” and “Paul Terry” — were allegedly written.
 A clairvoyant claimed the murder weapons were buried in woods on the Murdaugh family farm, 150 yards from the victims.
 A woman in some kind of rehab facility also said she had info on the murders, while another woman claimed that murder weapons were destroyed in a suspicious fire on Murdaugh family land.
 None of these tips were confirmed to be true.
 Meanwhile, other allegations reached SLED about supposed related crimes.
 One Lowcountry man claimed that Murdaugh helped his ex-wife obtain power of attorney over their cancer-stricken son, which then enabled her to steal tens of thousands of dollars raised for the son’s medical bills.
 Investigative notes indicate the woman made a withdrawal of $54,000 in 2014 and that Murdaugh allegedly told the father that it was illegal for more than one person to be listed on a power of attorney, which would be untrue.
 The case history also features notes about how the alleged thief and her boyfriend, who supposedly was involved in a former drug smuggling ring, allegedly voiced concern that police would question them about “buried money.”
 Prosecutors convicted Murdaugh of numerous instances of wrongdoing as a lawyer, but never charged anyone in regard to this allegation.
 No end to ‘Murdaugh madness’
 Prosecutors have alleged Murdaugh acted alone when slaughtering his wife and son.
 Since the killings, however, at least two allegations have been made that a small-town Lowcountry police chief helped transport and discard murder weapons and bloody clothing.
 In one instance, a former municipal judge in the Hampton County town of Yemassee alleged Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander helped Murdaugh conceal his alleged role in the killings by taking away incriminating evidence, including a shotgun, rifle and bloody clothes.
 The judge claimed Alexander and another police officer temporarily brought some of these items into the town police station soon after the murders. Three years after this tip was first shared with SLED, the law enforcement agency and prosecutors revisited the claim this summer and have shared alleged evidence with a state grand jury, which so far has not taken any action.
 The dog kennels at the Murdaugh family’s Moselle property on Wednesday, March 1, 2023 in Islandton.
 File/Staff 
 Another tip, contained in the case history, alleges that Alexander and another man bushwhacked a path through a wetlands area outside of Yemassee’s town limits in the weeks after the Murdaugh murders, possibly to dump weapons.
 Such allegations against Alexander are “ridiculous,” said Joe McCulloch, his Columbia-based lawyer.
 McCulloch said that the chief has no recollection of hacking through vegetation outside the town and also that his client had “no part in the hiding of murder weapons or other evidence.” McCulloch also said Alexander denies arriving at the murder scene before the official police response.
 The lawyer said these allegations are part of the “Murdaugh madness” associated with the sprawling case and its mini-universe of associated media, including documentaries, television shows, podcasts, blogs and books.
 “I think it’s impossible, absurd, and unsupported by everything, and denied by the chief,” McCulloch said of the accomplice allegations. “It’s sad the chief of police has to suffer this crap. He’s not happy about it.”
 McCulloch blamed unnamed “trolls” for spreading unfounded rumors and stirring a “mythical pot of conspiracy.” McCulloch said his client, who has not been charged with any Murdaugh-related crime, has not testified before a grand jury in regards to allegations of handling murder scene evidence.
 Given the specific allegation regarding the chief allegedly blazing a trail to a pond within wetlands, McCulloch said that police would have brought charges if there were any truth to the claim.
 “It is a non-allegation that we have to assume SLED fully investigated,” said McCulloch. “One would think that in two-and-one-half years, SLED would be out there with boats and divers and magnets…”
 SLED deployed divers in at least two places during its investigation of the murders, according to its case history.
 Divers searched a pond on the Murdaugh family farm about a week after the murders.
 Police dived again in February 2022 off a bridge on S.C. Highway 63. There they recovered a metal pipe that a man who was magnet fishing — using a high-powered magnet to retrieve sunken metal objects — apparently mistook for a shotgun barrel.
 When asked about its diving operations and if police searched the pond outside Yemassee, a SLED spokesperson said the agency “does not have any information to provide on this matter at this time” and suggested asking the S.C. Attorney General’s Office.
 The attorney general’s office did not answer questions about diving operations, either.
 “Our only comments on this case will be in court filings and hearings,” said spokesman Robert Kittle.
